title: Unpredictable costs of AI vs predictable cost of Humans

segments.text: Please give the biggest We Are
Developers welcome to Hung, Anna,
Leandro, and Raffi. LET'S GO!
>> [cheering]
[applause]
>> GREAT. UH CAN ANYBODY Everyone here is
okay at the back? Can you hear us?
Very good. Okay. Um so, this
conversation really started for me about
a couple of months ago when Uber CTO
came out on an interview and said,
"We've burned through all of our annual
token budget in 3 months."
And that kicked off an industry-wide
conversation on how fast companies are
spending tokens, how much it costs, and
me as a HR guy got me thinking, "Hang on
a minute. How does that balance with
human labor cost? How are we thinking
about the token cost on one side and
human payroll on the other?" And hence,
uh a couple months down the line, we
Here we are in Berlin talking about this
very topic. Um I'm delighted and honored
to be your moderator today. Uh my name
is Hung Lee. I write a newsletter called
Recruiting Brainfood. Um and yeah, it's
going to be a very interesting speaking
to these experts that I have either side
of me. So, let me introduce them real
quick. Uh Raffi, uh can you introduce
yourself? Who are you? What is you do?
>> Sure. Raffi Krikorian. I'm the CTO of
Mozilla.
>> Fantastic. Um Anna Ott?
>> Hi, I'm Anna. I work for a venture
capital firm. Uh so, I'm also more of
the HR side here.
>> Great stuff. And Leandro?
>> So, I'm Leandro Gomes da Silva, and I
help HR and TA teams to go from a
support function into a growth- and
revenue-driven function.
>> Yeah, fantastic stuff. These guys are
all on LinkedIn, so make sure you follow
them if you want more of their great
chat. Um Raffi, I'm going to start with
you. Um essentially, you are CTO of one
of the most uh famous technology
organizations on the planet.
I wondered if you could tell us a little
bit of a timeline as to how you've been
thinking about AI token budget over time
cuz we had a moment where it seemed that
token matching was a thing. Everybody
wanted to be AI enabled and then
suddenly AI agents emerged and are we
actually in control as to how fast we're
burning these tokens. Can you give us a
bit of a timeline as to how you've been
thinking about this?
>> Well, let me step back for a second
even. Like Mozilla is a very different
organization than what most people are
used to because we're actually a
portfolio of companies. So like that
means that we actually have a very
different uptake across every single one
of our organizations. Like something
like the Mozilla Corporation which
builds Firefox which I hope all of you
run. Um
has a policy in place where only humans
can commit to the code base. And that
actually fundamentally changes the way
tokens get used because we don't just
those two that team doesn't just let
agents run and do whatever they want
because they're meant to be in service
for a human actually committing the
code. Whereas the Mozilla AI Corporation
which is building developer facing
tooling, they don't write code anymore
as far as I can tell. Like all the
engineers are committing to specs and
then the CI build just does whatever it
does. So on that side we're burning
tokens like crazy on the Mozilla AI
side. But on the Mozilla Corporation
side, we're actually having an adoption
problem where like it's very spiky
throughout the organization. So like on
that end, we actually haven't burned
through our token budget yet yet. In
fact, we're still probably in the like
let's get more adoption. Let's figure
out what's the right way to use it. You
know, Fable and stuff aside, you know,
we've talked a lot about how Fable found
all these different bugs in the code
base. But on the Mozilla AI side, you
know, that one we're trying to figure
out how to like bring it back a little
bit of just like what actually are we
doing here? Who's actually writing code?
So for that, we're still on a
multi-month journey to figure it out, I
I
>> Yeah, so even even technology businesses
it's emerging scenario. We're all trying
to figure out as we go. Um, was there a
big moment in terms of how the pricing
of these leading models sort of shifted
from all you can eat type of usage to
now okay, it's priced on usage. Did that
drop like with you guys at the C-level
and think okay, we got to change
>> Yeah, so the so I'll tell two stories.
The Mozilla AI team has been running
analysis like crazy of just like if we
weren't doing this on subscriptions,
this would have cost us a lot of money
like kind of thing like all the money
we've infused into that company would be
kind of gone effectively right now. But
the Firefox team, you know, they very
famously used Fable to find 124 very
critical bugs inside Firefox. Those are
a lot of money per run. Let's say it
that way. I'm not sure I'm allowed to
disclose exactly how much money, but
it's a lot of money every time we do a
full-on Fable run across Firefox. So
like trying to balance like how many
times are going to run it versus how
many bugs versus okay, now we found all
these bugs we need to go fix them before
we run it again because we're trying to
manage that budget has become a real
conversation for us.
>> Yeah, really really interesting. Um, and
I want to bring you in on this
conversation here. Um, you're working as
a a kind of VP of people for a portfolio
company sort of for a VC that manages I
don't know how many startups.
>> 200? So okay, lots of money go to these
200 businesses. Um, how have the
investors been instructing or noting the
spend of that money? Um, and has that
changed over the last 5 years or so?
>> I think it starts with tech investors
being very very excited about it
themselves. So I think the first wave is
this will solve all our problems. This
will make every company more efficient
because we're going to be reducing costs
because we're reducing payroll. And then
every company will be better off, better
margins. Here are the glory days. And I
think then there was a day when we
realized a, the tools are not as
capable. B, is as we're just moving
money from payroll to token. And then
now we live in this more balanced,
probably third wave where we want to see
what are the big levers and use cases.
So we actually are getting more granular
in both conversations where we ask them,
okay, if you're burning tokens, which we
are not against, like what are the
outcomes? Like what is not only the
output and the outcome, but like what
are you really achieving with it? So
it's not like just people burning
through tokens um without any control or
any effects. So I think this is the what
we're seeing now that there's some
companies who actually have proof points
of where the use of AI has achieved
gains, whereas others just feel we're
just burning through money and we don't
see the overarching productivity. I also
have to say that I feel it's still a
single player game for most companies.
So the individual gets more productive,
but we don't see the
the um organizational-wide effects. Um
but I also want to say the
predictability is is unpredictable on
both sides because I'm also looking at
compensation and how that has changed
for people who are like frontier
professionals, the heavy users of AI.
You've probably seen this too. You might
still be hiring, but you don't know what
the cost of that person will be as
opposed to a year or two ago. So
wild west everywhere?
>> Yeah, I think that's right. I mean, the
title says predictable human costs, but
actually that's kind of strange. The
only things we ever kind of would
believe that a human being is
predictable. We know that compensation
is explicitly. There's all kinds of
implicit costs of hiring a human being.
>> Because there's supply demand. When you
think about compensation being driven by
supply demand and it's basically a price
tag on a person or role or a job. And
now jobs are
architecturally shifting. Uh developer
is no longer just a developer, right? So
how do we look at the new jobs that are
created? How do we look at the super IC
person that is producing so much more
outcome and is currently totally
breaking up our salary grid. How do we
price this? How do we price for impact
instead of time spent in the office? All
those things. So, we all are re-wiring
those systems as we speak, too. So, I
think next year we'll probably have more
answers, but this is where I find
compensation incredibly unpredictable. I
find human output at this point mostly
unpredictable. Organizational design
also being re-wired. So, it's
interesting to see what happens next,
but I'm with you. It's There's employers
who lure people in for unlimited token
use or you get 20k of token per year.
Those It's a thing that attracts talent,
for sure.
But, you also have to give them guidance
of like what should you use the tokens
for? Like, does it make sense to run
favor through all these things, right?
>> Yeah, I mean, that's why we have to do
it in a very judicious way. It's just
like we do the run, then we'll fix some
bugs, and then maybe we'll do another
run. Because there was I mean, like, if
you think about a world of like if right
now we live in this world where where
tokens are abundant, but they cost
something. If you try to think about the
what the scarcity world looks like, then
it becomes a token allocation problem.
Like, where do we want to spend those
tokens becomes like really the
interesting question for the engineering
managers to just like who's been the
most productive on that. Which teams
might be the most behind is a theory we
have. I don't know if it'll actually
work, but trying to figure out that
token allocation is an interesting
question.
>> Yeah, really interesting. Leandro, I'm
going to bring you in on this because
you're working in a different context,
smaller businesses, probably more
natural constraints in terms of what you
can spend. Can you tell us a little bit
about how you've kind of tried to figure
your way through
where to allocate the tokens, where to
use the technology, where you think
actually a human being is going to be a
better play?
>> Yeah, so I think taking one step back,
we need to reframe how we see the token
usage because we cannot say there is a
one-on-one comparison with a salary
compensation on a yearly basis, right?
Because we are all still figuring it
out. The technology is young. We're
trying to understand and train all of
the different programs.
If we look at what has a senior done,
what is the cost to get to a senior
level?
All over all those years, then it's a
completely different conversation,
right? So, what I've done is I've
noticed fairly quickly within smaller
companies that it's very hard to train
people on having a proper use of AI.
It's not one training, it's not five
training, it is something you need a
dedicated time for, you need to free up
people 10% of the time, yada yada yada.
I made a different decision. So, I
created something that's called AI
operations where basically I'm leading
that department and I'm putting the main
experts together with technical experts
to look at the actual problems you want
to solve. First look, what is the
process? Is that a process that still
holds in this AI future that we're
living in?
Is it an automation or an AI problem?
And only then you step to AI and when
it's AI, you're going to look at it from
the fundamental perspective, per
definition saving you tokens. So,
instead of just smacking mud against the
wall hoping that sticks,
no, we're looking at it from a
fundamental perspective, having a road
map, testing it within a
small environment, being very agile
about it,
uh reporting ROI and we kill experiments
that don't work. So, an experiment has
to prove its worth every 2 weeks and if
it's not, it's dead and we move on.
>> But we can agree that we need the
adolescence that we're in to figuring
out what is a stupid use and a good use
because I don't think we know clearly.
So, you have to experiment to come up
with like this is a idea, this is a
good idea, right?
>> That's true, but do you need to give
everyone your organization unlimited
tokens to do so? No, I don't think so. I
think you can centralize that, bring
people in, communicate with them so they
can co-create with you, but you have to
make a certain team responsible and
accountable for that token usage.
>> mean I can agree with that cuz like
we're in this world where it's like I
mean software engineering has always
been an art, not a science. And so we're
still figuring out the art of this
particular tool, which is why I kind of
like the way in Mozilla we like isolated
on a per company basis of just like you
try something different, you try
something different. At least we bounded
our blast radius, maybe.
>> You need to look for the overlap, right?
Because that's that's what where the
real value is, and you have that
centralized, and you have again for me
HR people, TA people are great
communicators. If you can centralize the
knowledge and make them talk the
different languages, and then translate
it to AI,
that's that's what I love what I do.
>> Um going back to you Raphael on this, um
how do you allocate a uh token budget uh
across all of these different
businesses? I mean, do you push it to
you decentralize that decision, so it's
basically up to the local managers?
>> No, I mean, I think we're still in this
experimental phase. And so, like I I do
not know. Like I do not know what an
ideal allocation looks like. So, every
single company is just trying something
different with the hopes that sometime
at the end of Q4, we'll probably have a
general sense of what's working or
what's not working, but right now we
literally do not know. It's kind of like
everyone try their own thing.
>> Can I Can I ask It's a a dark question,
so forgive me for that.
Allocation versus usage versus who's
using what? Because I've seen companies
who celebrate the people who burn
through the most tokens. It's like a
token user board, a leaderboard, and
then people is like, "Oh, these are the
obviously smartest people,
uh the furthest advance on the adoption
curve." And then there's also people who
just gamify this because we have seen
companies incentivizing this even. So,
how do you deal with this from
good use versus just random use to be on
the leaderboard kind of use?
>> I mean, we have this interesting
problem. Mozilla is 25 years old, right?
So, like we're not a young startup of
like people who just want to use AI all
the time. In fact, like my biggest
problem is actually convincing some of
the older engineers to actually go and
try it. So, the leaderboard for us has
actually been like an inverse thing of
us being able to ask people, "Why
haven't you actually just tried?" Like
you could have a valid reason. We'd love
to know what that reason is, but like
with more of a question like, "Why
haven't you tried?" Yes, we have one or
two like really far outliers that like
are building their own gas towns and
stuff like that in the corner that we
can then also ask them what's going on.
But like we're not in the place where
we're celebrating maximum maximizing.
We're in fact just looking at the
average and just understanding where
everyone is compared to that average.
Now again, Mozilla AI might be a very
different beast because like those guys
as far as I can tell aren't writing
code. And so like just like using them
as our petri dish of just like is this
even about like what's going to happen
to open source if like we don't write
code anymore. Like choosing them as my
experimental frontier has been
interesting. Ask me again in 6 months
and I'll tell you who works. Like I I'll
know.
>> Um Anna Ortese, I want to ask you a
question on the AI economy or at large.
A lot of it VC backed, a lot of it
backed by investment rather than
revenue.
Um what's your take on the AI bubble
narrative?
Um and
is AI basically fundamentally subsidized
such that actually what we're using
today maybe a lot more expensive than
what we're actually paying and at some
point that bill is going to come due.
>> Love the question.
Uh I have no precise answer because I
don't I'm old enough to have been living
through the first digital bubble in
2000. So I don't want to bring another
bubble back, but it might be inflated.
When I look at funding rounds definitely
it's hard to understand why there's so
much money allocated on some companies
that are very young
and very unclear. So there is this
sentiment that we're probably
creating something that is like an
inflation. Yes.
But when I look at the application layer
of AI companies we're seeing, we're also
seeing a type of companies in startups
that are created that haven't been
existing before. So we have subject
matter experts. So think real estate,
think health, think industry, like super
niche people who come out of their geek
niche and they suddenly get AI to build
a company and solve a real world problem
that I was never able to be solved. So
we are beyond the past where we see a
lot of consumer companies and generic
size of fintech companies. We suddenly
see super niche real world problems
being solved with AI by people who are
freaking experts on a very small thing
and that I actually celebrate.
So I don't know what of them will be
surviving. That's not for me to say.
It's venture capital.
Um
but I think there's a way that we see
business models emerging and found
archetypes emerging that are new and
they are relevant and they should have a
place.
>> Really good. I want to get Leandro's and
Raffi's view on this. Is AI subsidized
and we is the bill going to come due?
>> So the answer is simple answer is yes,
it is heavily subsidized.
Um it's not new. It was expected, right?
We need to get people hooked and often,
I hope I don't offend anyone, but it's
it's the heroin dealer.
It's our heroin dealer. You get a little
bit to try, it gets you hooked.
And once you want to leave, you can't.
You need that person. And that is what's
happening and we will start seeing We're
seeing it with Fable right now. Let's
give people a few days of Fable.
But once you've built something, you
want to continue building it. You go to
API calls and trust me, um your wallet's
not going to like that.
>> Really interesting. Raffi, as a as a as
a a C-level leader, are you thinking
about this as a from a business
continuity perspective and from a risk
perspective? Because
>> one of the things that we've been trying
out is like our I would love to get to
the place where our my engineers or
engineers across Mozilla are using
the best frontier quality models you
possibly can. But for the rest of the
organization, I don't think that needs
to be true. Like I don't I like I would
love our finance team to be using more
AI, but do they need to be making calls
to Fable? Do they need to be making even
calls to Opus? It's unclear. Like we can
go run and maybe even host some like
open source Chinese based models and let
them run against that with at a fraction
of the cost. So like I'm already looking
at tearing across our organization. Even
with I mean this is like a common
practice within application that you
should be clearly tearing, but I want to
be tearing across the entire org so that
we make sure that we're like just
managing that budget a bit more because
you're right. I mean, like the word user
is only used by drug dealers and tech
people, right? So like So like we need
to figure out how to make sure that that
gets properly managed. Like I used to
work at Uber. It was significantly
cheaper to ride Uber pre-pre IPO. Post
IPO, the price has changed. The exact
same thing is going to happen here.
>> Yeah, really good. I want to go back to
model routing in a second, Raffi, but
talking about rewiring workflows to a
level of AI cost that may actually
escalate in future. Anna, is that a
conversation happening anywhere within
the portfolio that you're in? For
instance, you might have companies that
are building a process, firing a
department because, "Hey, listen, we can
do it faster here and cheaper here." But
are they thinking, "You know what? 5
years down the line, this may cost like
twice the amount of the people you
fired."
>> I'm generally but concerned about people
who think that that they know what the
future looks like.
So I think workforce planning, for
example, which is a good example, is we
have done this in a 12-month cadence and
then now it's like a quarterly basis
because it's only how far we can look.
So for example, the question is, do we
need more seniors? Do we need more
juniors? Do we actually need developers?
What is a developer? Those kind of
questions. I don't think that anyone has
a clear answer. So you need to take it
bit by bit and what you know and you
have to experiment and look at the data
and the usage and all the things. Build
a model for your firm that makes sense
so you can figure out what you need and
what you don't need. And then there's
also the cost element to it, obviously.
But when I think about
founders laying off entire teams and
this makes a lot of headlines,
obviously,
I think they might be reworking some of
this. And also there's examples out
there who already have been reworking
some of it. Like, do we fire all HR or
customer service people and then bring
some back? So I think there's a bit of
an ebb and flow and there's not an
advantage to being too much of an early
adopter here. So, the balance is more
important. I think Europe is a bit more
balanced here, I think, because it's
also harder to let go of talent, which I
sometimes find
helpful. What I do see, though, is less
backfill hiring. So, everyone who leaves
won't be replaced. Some will. They will
be replaced differently.
Um the org chart is no longer pyramid. I
think about it more like a hot dog.
There's more Some people in the top, few
juniors, and a fat master sausage layer
in the middle of like super senior ICs.
It's It's a thing. It's a You will be
thinking about this. So, no pyramids,
more hot dogs.
Succession benches will be empty because
it's kind of going to be harder for
juniors to break in.
And last thing, more scrutiny on the
exact layer because I don't know how the
token usage correlates with your levels.
We see founders living in Claude,
juniors gaining so much through Claude,
and then some of the exact layer in
between getting totally frustrated and
overwhelmed and surpassed by the bottom.
So, there's probably less leadership
need sometime. I don't know.
>> Yeah, I can imagine that. I mean, that
kind of makes sense in the
people who've basically had a career
successfully pre-AI, they may have more
to lose with the changing world, right?
So, a younger person coming in, they've
got nothing to lose. They're going to
just go to the new. So, I totally get
that the middle part of that previous
pyramid probably is most vulnerable.
Leandro, what are you on this cuz you've
worked with a lot of the companies that
probably are going through this process
right now. Um how are you kind of
observing like what's your observations
as to how that that top, middle, and
junior sort of pyramid stacking? Like
who's using, who's winning, who's
losing?
>> So,
what we've all been seeing in the
market, and now there's there are
reports emerging from places like
Gartner BCG looking back at what
happened the last 2 3 years with all of
these layoffs. So, going back to your
previous point, actually the impact is
minimal of replacing people for AI, the
impact is minimal. So, that's the wrong
approach. We know that. What is the
right approach? No one knows yet. One
thing we do need to realize is a job is
more than a bunch of tasks. And there's
a lot of intricacies there. And how we
will measure it? Again, we're trying to
figure that out. What we clearly see,
everyone sees that, is the junior
problem, right? I I have Uber drivers
telling me, "I'm a software engineer. I
graduated. I can't find a job."
And that's where again I'm going back to
my AI operations model where I say we
need to get these people in with domain
experts because they are cheaper than
the super senior ones to start building
at the fundamental issues, the
fundamental processes that we're facing.
I see that as a potential solution to
part of that problem.
Um middle managers have it
Yeah, busier than ever. Um we can do
much more because of AI.
But what do we do? And because we can do
much more, we can wear many more hats,
people are getting burnout because of
working too much and having too many
options. So, we need to really balance
this and and try to define like, yes, we
should use AI. Yes, we should use a lot
of it to be efficient. But what is the
impact of that on the person? And I
think that's really important.
>> I heard the other day that there's
startups in Silicon Valley have like
sickness rooms where people go if they
overdose on AI. It's a problem. And
touch grass part, please. There should
be something in Berlin, by the way.
>> have to say what what I have noticed is
the people really thriving in AI, the
builders,
it's a lot of neurodiverse people. Like,
I for example, I have ADHD. It's
amazing. I've never been able to be so
focused because the game is changing
almost every day. So, you're focused on
building with the latest and greatest.
But that's a small part of the
population, right? The rest is
overloaded with context switching, all
of those things. And we really need to
think about that impact as well.
>> There's statistics that say 30% of
founders most likely have diagnosed or
undiagnosed ADHD, so it's a niche only
somewhere.
>> Yeah.
Uh Rafi, I want to bring you in on this.
Uh you mentioned at the right at the
beginning of the the panel that Mozilla
has been around 25 years. That's a
that's a huge amount of time for a tech
company, um and presumably there is like
in the DNA of the organization that you
want to keep going for another 25, 30,
50 years going forward. But how do we do
that? Um by making sure that we have
that early entry floor of talent because
there is a perception that AI can do
some of the repetitive work at the
junior level. We don't need to hire at
the bottom. We're just going to keep on
with the AI spend. How are you wrestling
with that conundrum?
>> I mean, Mozilla is it just a different
beast, right? We're not a for-profit
corporation. We're a nonprofit that's
very community-focused. So in fact, like
us hiring junior engineers for us is a
win because we want junior we want the
junior engineers to be on the front
lines talking to committers who are not
part of Mozilla. We want them to be on
the front lines talking to people
understanding what are new opportunities
for us to go and build third-way
technologies that can change the the way
the marketplace works, the way the
incentives work. So in fact, for us like
this might be a winning proposition for
us cuz we want those junior people to be
that front line for us because I don't
think a I don't think community's going
to be want to be built by AI bots
talking to them every single day.
They're going to want human interaction,
and that human interaction gets us intel
on the kinds of stuff that Mozilla needs
to build to make the world a better
place. So for us, I think we're in a
very unique place um and a very grateful
being in this place. If we were if we
were being a purely capitalistic-driven
company, we'd have a very different
equation on that.
>> Well, you know, it's really interesting
you mentioned about the structure of the
organization. I do think this AI moment
is going to lead to a proliferation
of different ways in which we're going
to structure human uh organizations
essentially. There'll be more co-ops,
there'll be more community-driven type
work, there'll be more
different types of construction to put
this labor together because I think that
ultimately, as you say, the pure
for-profit capitalist way, maybe that's
going to grind down to zero at some
point. And I don't
>> Yeah, we had this chat before we went on
stage where
in my role I help companies figure out
what's the best org chart, what kind of
talent they need,
what hiring needs they should generally
look for, what are all the things. And I
think my advice is so dated that I
sometimes don't know, like how many SDRs
or AEs do you need? How many developers?
Like I don't know these things. And yes,
once we find out I think we will be have
a better bigger variety of companies
than we have seen so far. There was one
SaaS playbook, there was one fintech
playbook. It was a clear
departmentalization of like this is
product, this is engine, this is why
this exists. And now it's all merged and
differently component. And I think it's
interesting to see how it does, but I
think at the end of it that we will have
different organizations running
completely different in hybrid models
and different org chart designs with
juniors, which is more
